claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data showing strong adaptation and rate-dependent responses in DKO SGNs (Figure 7).

claims.claim: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels is a pivotal initiator of neurotransmission.
claims.source: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels (CaVs) is a pivotal initiator of neurotransmission.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about synaptic transmission.

claims.claim: Voltage-gated calcium channels typically undergo considerable Ca2+- and voltage-dependent inactivation.
claims.source: These channels typically undergo considerable Ca2+- and voltage-dependent inactivation (CDI and VDI), which limits the amount of incoming Ca2+ ions and thus possible excitotoxicity.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about calcium channel biophysics.

claims.claim: In sensory inner hair cells, the extent of calcium channel inactivation is significantly reduced.
claims.source: In sensory receptor cells such as sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and photoreceptors, however, the extent of inactivation is significantly reduced to allow encoding of graded and sustained membrane potential fluctuations in response to ongoing sound or visual (t.i. 'darkness') stimuli (reviewed in Pangrsic et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Pangrsic et al., 2018).

claims.claim: In photoreceptors, the extent of calcium channel inactivation is significantly reduced.
claims.source: In sensory receptor cells such as sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) and photoreceptors, however, the extent of inactivation is significantly reduced to allow encoding of graded and sustained membrane potential fluctuations in response to ongoing sound or visual (t.i. 'darkness') stimuli (reviewed in Pangrsic et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review article (Pangrsic et al., 2018).

claims.claim: Slowed inactivation of L-type CaVs was reported at ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, slowed inactivation of L-type CaVs was also reported at ribbon synapses of retinal bipolar cells (von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1996), which transmit visual information via continuous exocytosis of synaptic vesicles onto retinal ganglion cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to von Gersdorff and Matthews, 1996.

claims.claim: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs.
claims.source: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which primarily abate the calmodulin (CaM)-mediated CDI of CaV channels (Haeseleer et al., 2000; Findeisen and Minor, 2010; Haeseleer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CaBP function.

claims.claim: CaBPs primarily abate the calmodulin-mediated CDI of CaV channels.
claims.source: The attenuation of channel inactivation may be largely attributed to the action of calcium-binding proteins, CaBPs (Haeseleer et al., 2000), which primarily abate the calmodulin (CaM)-mediated CDI of CaV channels (Haeseleer et al., 2000; Findeisen and Minor, 2010; Haeseleer et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on CaBP-CaM interactions.

claims.claim: At IHC ribbon synapses, the Ca2+ current is carried through L-type CaV1.3 channels.
claims.source: At the IHC ribbon synapses, the Ca2+ current is carried through the L-type CaV1.3 channels (Baig et al., 2011; Platzer et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baig et al., 2011 and Platzer et al., 2000.

claims.claim: CaV1.3 channel biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members.
claims.source: Their biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018), but most prominently by CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: CaV1.3 channel biophysical properties are most prominently regulated by CaBP2.
claims.source: Their biophysical properties may be regulated by several CaBP family members (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018), but most prominently by CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claims.claim: The loss of CaBP2 significantly affects VDI but not CDI of IHC Ca2+ currents.
claims.source: Interestingly, the loss of CaBP2 seems to significantly affect VDI, but not CDI of the IHC Ca2+ currents (Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claims.claim: Isolated disruption of CaBP1 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation.
claims.source: Furthermore, isolated disruption of CaBP1 or CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Isolated disruption of CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation.
claims.source: Furthermore, isolated disruption of CaBP1 or CaBP4 in mice leads to at most modest enhancement of IHC CaV1.3 inactivation (Cui et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cui et al., 2007 and Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform is abundant at IHC ribbon synapses.
claims.source: Moreover, the automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform, abundant at the IHC ribbon synapses (Bock et al., 2011; Scharinger et al., 2015), does not seem critical for CDI suppression either, as its disruption does not lead to hearing impairment (Scharinger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bock et al., 2011 and Scharinger et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform does not seem critical for CDI suppression.
claims.source: Moreover, the automodulatory C-terminal domain of the long CaV1.3 isoform, abundant at the IHC ribbon synapses (Bock et al., 2011; Scharinger et al., 2015), does not seem critical for CDI suppression either, as its disruption does not lead to hearing impairment (Scharinger et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Scharinger et al., 2015.

claims.claim: CaBP2 is the most abundant member of the CaBP family in the cochlea.
claims.source: Since CaBP2, followed by the structurally similar CaBP1, are the most abundant members of the CaBP family in the cochlea (Yang et al., 2016), we set out to investigate the phenotype of Cabp1/2 double-knockout (DKO) animals at the systems and cellular levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: CaBP1 is the second most abundant member of the CaBP family in the cochlea.
claims.source: Since CaBP2, followed by the structurally similar CaBP1, are the most abundant members of the CaBP family in the cochlea (Yang et al., 2016), we set out to investigate the phenotype of Cabp1/2 double-knockout (DKO) animals at the systems and cellular levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Severe hearing impairment was observed in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
claims.source: Severe hearing impairment that we observed in these animals reveals that CaBP1 and 2 act together to attenuate the inactivation of the IHC CaV1.3 channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained exocytosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes the fast component of exocytosis.
claims.source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that the combined absence of CaBP1 and 2 almost abolishes sustained, and, upon increased hair cell synaptic activity, the fast component of exocytosis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements at different holding potentials shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp1 single KO animals.
claims.source: Such phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp2 single KO animals.
claims.source: Such phenotype was observed neither in Cabp1 nor in Cabp2 single KO animals (Yang et al., 2018; Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Picher, 2017.

claims.claim: Viral delivery of Cabp2 coding sequence resulted in substantial recovery of hearing in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
claims.source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ABR data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 restored Ca2+ currents in Cabp1/2 double-knockout IHCs.
claims.source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figures 1-4.

claims.claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 restored IHC exocytosis in Cabp1/2 double-knockout animals.
claims.source: These experiments revealed a substantial recovery of hearing, which may be related to the successful restoration of Ca2+ currents and IHC exocytosis upon transgenic expression of CaBP2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The functions of CaBP1 and 2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse.
claims.source: Our findings indicate that the functions of CaBP1 and 2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that single knockouts have milder phenotypes than the double knockout.

claims.claim: CaBP1 and 2 together provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at IHC synapses.
claims.source: Together, they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise, indefatigable neurotransmission at this synapse.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the combined data from patch-clamp recordings and in vivo SGN recordings.

claims.claim: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization show pronounced inactivation in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs compared to WT.
claims.source: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization step to the maximum current potential in the apical IHCs of WT and Cabp1/2-DKO animals. Note a pronounced inactivation of the Ca2+ current in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 and partial recovery upon Cabp2 gene replacement.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Cabp2 gene replacement leads to partial recovery of Ca2+ current inactivation in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
claims.source: Peak normalized Ca2+ currents after a 500-ms depolarization step to the maximum current potential in the apical IHCs of WT and Cabp1/2-DKO animals. Note a pronounced inactivation of the Ca2+ current in the absence of CaBP1 and 2 and partial recovery upon Cabp2 gene replacement.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The fraction of remaining Ca2+ current after 500-ms depolarization is significantly lower in Cabp1/2-DKO compared to WT, Cabp1-KO, and Cabp2-KO.
claims.source: The fraction of the remaining Ca2+ current after a 500-ms depolarization step is depicted for different mouse models acquired at comparable conditions (room temperature, 2 mM extracellular [Ca2+]). The histogram combines the results of this study (Cabp1/2-DKO) with previously published data on CaBP1 (Yang et al., 2018) and CaBP2 (Picher, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C comparing different genotypes.

claims.claim: Ca2+ currents are reduced upon a train of 10-ms long depolarization steps in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
claims.source: Ca2+ currents upon a train of 10-ms long depolarization steps normalized to the amplitude of the first pulse.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Ca2+-current amplitudes are slightly reduced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals transduced with PHP.eB-Cabp2.
claims.source: Ca2+-current–voltage relationships show slightly reduced amplitudes in the IHCs of the Cabp1/2-DKO animals transduced with the PHP.eB-Cabp2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: There is a significant difference in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) between CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and controls (p < 0.0001).
claims.source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of activation curves shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: There is a significant difference in the slope of activation curves between CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and controls (p < 0.0001).
claims.source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of activation curves shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The voltage shift in activation persists upon re-expression of CaBP2 in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
claims.source: Note a significant difference (asterisks,p < 0.0001, Student's t-test) in the half-voltage activation (V0.5) and slope in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs and the persistence of the voltage shift upon re-expression of CaBP2 (inserts).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: VDI is significantly enhanced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (p < 0.0001).
claims.source: VDI and CDI were both significantly enhanced in the IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (asterisks; Student's t-test, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: CDI is significantly enhanced in IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (p < 0.0001).
claims.source: VDI and CDI were both significantly enhanced in the IHCs of Cabp1/2-DKO animals (asterisks; Student's t-test, p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: VDI in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs is approximately two times larger than in WT IHCs (0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02).
claims.source: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs (Figure 2B; VDI: 0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02 and CDI: 0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: CDI in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs is approximately six times larger than in WT IHCs (0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02).
claims.source: The lack of CaBP1 and 2 significantly enhanced both, VDI and CDI of IHC CaV1.3 channels, which were approx. two and six times larger than those in WT IHCs (Figure 2B; VDI: 0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02 and CDI: 0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02 in Cabp1/2 DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.0001, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In response to short stimuli, capacitance increases were comparable between WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
claims.source: In response to short stimuli [primarily recruiting the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles], increases in capacitance were comparable, while long stimuli (reporting sustained exocytosis) evoked significantly smaller responses in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (Figure 3A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Long stimuli evoked significantly smaller capacitance responses in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs compared to WT.
claims.source: In response to short stimuli [primarily recruiting the readily releasable pool (RRP) of vesicles], increases in capacitance were comparable, while long stimuli (reporting sustained exocytosis) evoked significantly smaller responses in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (Figure 3A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by capacitance measurements shown in Figure 3A, B.

claims.claim: Peak Ca2+-current amplitudes are comparable between WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
claims.source: These results are in line with the observation of comparable peak Ca2+-current amplitudes but reduced calcium charge transfer (QCa) for stimulus durations above 50 ms.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Calcium charge transfer (QCa) is reduced for stimulus durations above 50 ms in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
claims.source: These results are in line with the observation of comparable peak Ca2+-current amplitudes but reduced calcium charge transfer (QCa) for stimulus durations above 50 ms.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot completely be explained by the diminished Ca2+ influx in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs.
claims.source: However, calculating exocytosis efficiency revealed that the reduction in sustained exocytosis cannot completely be explained by the diminished Ca2+ influx (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of exocytosis efficiency shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There is an additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs beyond reduced Ca2+ influx.
claims.source: This suggests an additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes, the underlying mechanism of which is currently unknown.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that exocytosis efficiency is reduced beyond what would be expected from reduced Ca2+ influx.

claims.claim: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs.
claims.source: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 largely restored the efficiency of exocytosis, indicating that the impairment as observed in the IHCs of DKOs is related to the absence of the CaBPs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The exocytosis defect observed in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs was not observed in Cabp2-KOs when IHCs are held at hyperpolarized potential at room temperature.
claims.source: Such exocytosis defect was not observed in Cabp2-KOs, suggesting that when IHCs are held at hyperpolarized potential at RT, CaBP1 provides sufficient compensation to obscure the synaptic phenotype (Picher, 2017; Oestreicher et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Picher, 2017 and Oestreicher et al., 2021.

claims.claim: CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs showed significant impairment of sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step) compared to WT controls.
claims.source: CaBP1/2-deficient inner hair cells (IHCs) showed significant impairment of the sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step, respectively) and reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) as compared to WT controls (black asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs showed reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) compared to WT controls.
claims.source: CaBP1/2-deficient inner hair cells (IHCs) showed significant impairment of the sustained exocytosis (p < 0.05 for 20 ms, and <0.001 for 100- and 200-ms step, respectively) and reduced cumulative Ca2+ influx (p < 0.005 for the longest two pulses) as compared to WT controls (black asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: AAV-mediated delivery of Cabp2 improved IHC synaptic function as compared to non-injected Cabp1/2-DKO controls (p < 0.01 for ΔCm upon 100- and 200-ms step, and p < 0.05 for QCa upon 200-ms step).
claims.source: AAV-mediated delivery of Cabp2 improved IHC synaptic function as compared to non-injected Cabp1/2-DKO controls (p < 0.01 for ΔCm upon 100- and 200-ms step, and p < 0.05 for QCa upon 200-ms step; green asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: There is a reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (p < 0.005 for the two longest test pulses).
claims.source: Note a reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis (p < 0.005 for the two longest test pulses; black asterisks), which can be efficiently rescued by intracochlear delivery of PHP.eB-Cabp2 (p < 0.01 and 0.05 for 100- and 200-ms pulse, respectively; green asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Intracochlear delivery of PHP.eB-Cabp2 efficiently rescues the reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis (p < 0.01 and 0.05 for 100- and 200-ms pulse, respectively).
claims.source: Note a reduced efficiency of Ca2+-dependent exocytosis (p < 0.005 for the two longest test pulses; black asterisks), which can be efficiently rescued by intracochlear delivery of PHP.eB-Cabp2 (p < 0.01 and 0.05 for 100- and 200-ms pulse, respectively; green asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between test pulses.
claims.source: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between the test pulses (p < 0.01 for 50 ms, and p < 0.005 for 20-, 100-, and 200-ms pulse) and a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: At –55 mV holding potential, there is a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).
claims.source: Capacitance measurements at a holding potential of –55 mV reveal an aggravation of the phenotype by additional activation of calcium channels between the test pulses (p < 0.01 for 50 ms, and p < 0.005 for 20-, 100-, and 200-ms pulse) and a further discrepancy between the QCa of WT and CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs (2–10 ms: p < 0.05; 20–200 ms: p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) compared to non-injected controls at –55 mV holding potential.
claims.source: Also in these recording conditions, the IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) and exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) as compared to non-injected controls.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) compared to non-injected controls at –55 mV holding potential.
claims.source: Also in these recording conditions, the IHCs from Cabp2-injected Cabp1/2-DKO animals showed increased QCa (20–200 ms: p < 0.05) and exocytosis (100–200 ms: p < 0.005) as compared to non-injected controls.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a 60 ± 4% reduction in maximal Ca2+ currents in DKO IHCs.
claims.source: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a significant reduction in the maximal Ca2+ currents, which was more pronounced in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs as compared to controls (60 ± 4% vs 25 ± 4% reduction in DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.005, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 3D, E.

claims.claim: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a 25 ± 4% reduction in maximal Ca2+ currents in WT IHCs.
claims.source: Raising the holding voltage to –55 mV resulted in a significant reduction in the maximal Ca2+ currents, which was more pronounced in the CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs as compared to controls (60 ± 4% vs 25 ± 4% reduction in DKO and WT IHCs, respectively; p < 0.005, Student's t-test).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from experiments shown in Figure 3D, E.

claims.claim: At –55 mV holding potential, there was a complete loss of sustained exocytosis in DKO IHCs (p < 0.005).
claims.source: Consequently, further discrepancy between the QCa in IHCs of WT and DKO animals was observed (p < 0.001), which in DKO animals resulted in a complete loss of sustained exocytosis (Figure 3D; p < 0.005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: AAV-mediated transgenic expression of CaBP2 restored sustained exocytosis at –55 mV holding potential (p < 0.05).
claims.source: The latter was well restored upon AAV-mediated transgenic expression of CaBP2 (p < 0.05), which also reduced the amount of calcium channel inactivation (38 ± 8% reduction in the maximal Ca2+ current as well as a partial recovery of QCa as compared to Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: AAV-mediated transgenic expression of CaBP2 reduced calcium channel inactivation (38 ± 8% reduction in maximal Ca2+ current) at –55 mV holding potential.
claims.source: The latter was well restored upon AAV-mediated transgenic expression of CaBP2 (p < 0.05), which also reduced the amount of calcium channel inactivation (38 ± 8% reduction in the maximal Ca2+ current as well as a partial recovery of QCa as compared to Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative ABR data.

claims.claim: Upon 80 dB SPL click stimulation, no sizable ABR wave I was detected in average traces of DKO animals at either age tested.

claims.claim: The absence of ABR wave I suggests reduced and/or desynchronized spiking of spiral ganglion neurons.

claims.claim: Later ABR peaks were better preserved in Cabp1/2-DKO animals, indicating partially preserved activation of neurons of the auditory brainstem.

claims.claim: Cochlear amplification by outer hair cells is largely preserved in DKO animals.

claims.claim: In WT mice, 39 neurons were recorded and classified as SGNs based on their location, response patterns, spike waveforms and recording stability.

claims.source: In response to 50- or 500-ms tone burst at the characteristic frequency 30 dB above threshold (i.e. where the sigmoidal rate-intensity functions have saturated spike rates) and at a stimulus repetition rate of 5 or 0.5 Hz, they showed the SGN-typical very high onset firing rates, gradually adapting to reach steady-state rates between 100 and 400 Hz (Figure 7A, B).

claims.source: In contrast, only one out of the 20 neurons we recorded and analyzed from DKO animals showed a normal response in our automated tuning curve algorithm with a threshold of 35 dB SPL at 7.8 kHz, while all others displayed thresholds above 80 dB SPL and extremely low spike rates (Figure 7A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by single-unit recording data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claims.claim: In the majority of DKO neurons, frequency tuning was very broad.
claims.source: Since in the majority of neurons frequency tuning was very broad, we used subjectively chosen best frequency tone burst or white noise burst stimulation of at least 80 dB SPL for subsequent characterization.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental observations from single-unit recordings.

claims.source: 16 out of 19 DKO units responded with a relatively high onset rate but strong adaptation to a minimal sustained spiking (Figure 7A, B), which prevented unit classification based on the response patterns.

results.result: CaBP1 and CaBP2 double knockout mice exhibit dramatically enhanced voltage-dependent and calcium-dependent inactivation of CaV1.3 channels in inner hair cells. VDI increased approximately 2-fold (0.30 ± 0.02 vs 0.13 ± 0.02) and CDI increased approximately 6-fold (0.65 ± 0.01 vs 0.11 ± 0.02) compared to WT (p < 0.0001). Transgenic CaBP2 expression partially rescued this phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C13-14, C46-48, C54-57 collectively demonstrate enhanced channel inactivation in DKO mice through patch-clamp recordings (Figures 1-2). The quantitative measurements show statistically significant increases in both VDI and CDI with appropriate controls and statistical tests. The partial rescue by CaBP2 expression provides additional support for the causal role of CaBPs.

results.result: Sustained exocytosis is severely impaired in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs, particularly during prolonged stimulation and at depolarized holding potentials. The impairment exceeds what would be expected from reduced Ca2+ influx alone, suggesting additional defects in exo- or endocytic processes. AAV-mediated CaBP2 expression substantially rescued exocytosis efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C37-38, C58-79 are supported by capacitance measurements (Figure 3) showing impaired sustained exocytosis with appropriate statistical comparisons. The observation that exocytosis efficiency is reduced beyond Ca2+ influx reduction (C62-63) is supported by quantitative analysis. The rescue experiments (C64, C68-70, C73-74, C78-79) provide strong evidence for CaBP involvement. The holding potential experiments (C71-79) demonstrate activity-dependent worsening of the phenotype.

results.result: Recovery from CaV1.3 inactivation is slowed in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs, particularly after prolonged mild stimulation. After 500-ms depolarization, recovery time constants were 0.62 s (DKO) vs 0.75 s (WT). After 2-min sine wave stimulation, recovery was slowest in DKO IHCs, suggesting channels enter a 'deep-state' of inactivation with very slow recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C82-89 are supported by recovery experiments (Figure 4, Table 1) with quantitative kinetic measurements. The data show differential recovery kinetics depending on stimulation protocol. However, the interpretation of 'deep-state' inactivation (C89) is somewhat speculative, though supported by citations to similar phenomena in other channels. The paradoxical faster recovery after strong depolarization in DKO vs rescued cells (C86) requires mechanistic explanation provided by the authors.

results.result: Spiral ganglion neuron responses in vivo are severely impaired in Cabp1/2-DKO mice, showing drastically reduced spontaneous and sound-evoked spike rates, increased latency (12.5 ± 2.8 ms vs 4.8 ± 0.2 ms, p < 0.001), increased jitter (18.3 ± 5.0 vs 1.5 ± 0.4, p < 0.00001), and strong rate-dependent adaptation. Responses improved at lower stimulation rates (0.5 Hz vs 5 Hz).
results.evaluation: Claims C8-10, C118-138 are supported by in vivo single-unit recordings (Figure 7) with appropriate statistical analyses. The data show consistent impairments across multiple measures (spike rates, latency, jitter, adaptation). The rate-dependence (C126-128) provides strong evidence linking cellular channel inactivation to systems-level dysfunction. The low experimental yield (C133) and interpretation of silent neurons (C134) are reasonable inferences from the data.

results.result: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 via AAV-PHP.eB vector leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity in Cabp1/2-DKO mice. ABR thresholds improved significantly, click-evoked ABR amplitudes increased, and wave I latency shortened. However, thresholds did not completely recover to WT levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-12, C41-43, C115-117, C164-166, C222 are supported by comprehensive rescue experiments including patch-clamp recordings (Figures 1-4) and ABR measurements (Figure 6). The partial nature of the rescue (C166) is appropriately acknowledged. The data demonstrate both cellular and systems-level improvements, providing strong evidence for the causal role of CaBPs and potential for gene therapy.

results.result: Cabp1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe hearing impairment with highly elevated ABR thresholds. In young (3-4 week old) animals, tone bursts up to 90 dB SPL barely elicited responses. Click responses were better preserved (59 ± 2 dB SPL in DKO vs 30 ± 2 dB SPL in WT) but greatly reduced in amplitude. No sizable ABR wave I was detected, suggesting reduced/desynchronized SGN spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C36, C104-111 are supported by ABR measurements (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with appropriate controls and statistical analyses. The absence of wave I (C109) with preserved later peaks (C111) is consistent with IHC synapse dysfunction. The quantitative threshold measurements provide clear evidence of severe hearing impairment.

results.result: Immunohistochemistry reveals normal presynaptic CaV1.3 clustering and ribbon synapse abundance in Cabp1/2-DKO mice at 3 weeks, but increased intensities of pre- and postsynaptic markers. BK channel clusters appeared smaller in DKO IHCs (p < 0.0001) with reduced cumulative volume (6.6 ± 1.1 vs 14.2 ± 2.1 µm³ per IHC, p < 0.01). SK2 and BK maturation appeared normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-93, C96-101 are supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry (Figure 5) with appropriate statistical analyses. The normal synapse number (C91) but altered marker intensities (C92-93) and BK cluster size (C98-101) suggest compensatory changes. The normal maturation markers (C96-97) indicate developmental progression is not grossly disrupted. Sample sizes and statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse. The sole loss of either CaBP1 or CaBP2 can be largely compensated by the other, but together they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca²⁺ currents and exocytosis required for temporally precise neurotransmission.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-45, C143, C172-173 are supported by comparison of single knockout phenotypes (cited from prior work) with the severe DKO phenotype demonstrated in this study. The inference of partial redundancy is logical given that single knockouts have milder phenotypes than the double knockout. This is a key conceptual conclusion supported by the totality of the data.

results.result: Cochlear amplification by outer hair cells is largely preserved in Cabp1/2-DKO animals. In about half of DKO animals, DPOAEs were normal, while in the other half they were reduced in amplitude but still detectable.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-114 are supported by DPOAE measurements (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F). The data indicate that the hearing impairment is primarily due to IHC synapse dysfunction rather than outer hair cell dysfunction, which is important for localizing the defect. The variability between animals is appropriately noted.

results.result: CaBP1 and CaBP2 are highly abundant in inner hair cells and are the most abundant members of the CaBP family in the murine cochlea, while levels of CaBP4 and CaBP5 are negligible.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-2, C34-35, C144-145 are supported by citations to expression studies (Yang et al., 2016; Jean et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2022). This provides the rationale for focusing on CaBP1 and CaBP2 in the double knockout study. The claims accurately represent prior published work.

results.result: In vivo, in the absence of CaBP1 and 2, a large fraction of IHC CaV1.3 channels are predicted to be in prolonged inactivation, not supporting sufficient exocytosis for sustained sensory coding. The extent of channel inactivation and exocytosis impairment aggravates with the extent of IHC stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-81, C139-140, C203-206 represent predictions and interpretations based on in vitro data at different holding potentials (Figure 3) and in vivo SGN recordings (Figure 7). The predictions are reasonable extrapolations from the experimental data, though they involve some speculation about in vivo conditions. The activity-dependent worsening (C139-140) is directly supported by experimental data.

results.result: The mechanisms by which CaBPs may affect processes beyond channel inactivation remain unclear. CaBPs may directly regulate BK expression (e.g., as transcription factors) or indirectly through Ca²⁺ signaling. CaBPs may affect exocytosis through coupling of CaV1.3 channels and vesicles or regulation of other synaptic proteins. Future studies are needed to identify additional CaBP interaction partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-103, C185, C188, C192 represent hypotheses and proposals for future research rather than established findings. While the observations of reduced BK expression (C100-101) and exocytosis efficiency beyond Ca²⁺ influx (C62-63) are supported, the mechanistic explanations remain speculative. These are appropriate areas for future investigation but not currently supported conclusions.

results.result: Clinical implications for DFNB93: Synaptic activity in everyday sounds could inactivate calcium channels and reduce SGN spiking in patients. Communication in daily life may be more impaired than audiometric data suggest. Patients might benefit more from technologies improving signal-to-noise ratio than from simple amplification. Gene therapy may be a future treatment approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C216-221 represent clinical predictions and recommendations based on the mouse model data. While the predictions are reasonable extrapolations from the DKO phenotype, they remain speculative regarding human DFNB93 patients. The recommendations (C218-220) are logical but not directly tested. The gene therapy proposal (C221) is supported by the rescue experiments in mice but requires validation in humans.

results.result: There is a significant shift in the voltage dependence of CaV1.3 activation in CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs toward more hyperpolarized values (V0.5: -33.6 ± 0.5 mV vs -30.9 ± 0.5 mV, p < 0.0001) and increased slope (7.6 ± 0.1 vs 7.1 ± 0.1, p < 0.0001). This voltage shift persists upon CaBP2 re-expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-53 are supported by quantitative analysis of activation curves (Figure 1F) with appropriate statistical tests. However, the authors note this finding is surprising and opposite to expectations from heterologous expression systems, suggesting potential compensatory changes in channel composition. The persistence of the shift after rescue (C53) is an interesting observation that warrants further investigation.

results.result: The kinetics of recovery from inactivation may reflect different processes depending on stimulation protocol. Recovery after 500-ms depolarization may reflect Ca²⁺ clearance kinetics, while recovery after prolonged sine wave may reflect channel recovery from slow inactivation. CaBP2 may act as a slow mobile calcium buffer, and overexpressed CaBP2 may prolong Ca²⁺ clearance.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-199 represent mechanistic interpretations and hypotheses to explain the complex recovery kinetics observed in Figure 4 and Table 1. While the data showing differential recovery kinetics are solid, the mechanistic explanations involve considerable speculation. The hypotheses are plausible and supported by citations to related work, but direct experimental evidence for these specific mechanisms is lacking. The authors appropriately suggest future experiments combining patch-clamp with calcium imaging.

results.result: In Cabp1/2 double-knockout (DKO) mice, CaV1.3 channel inactivation is strongly enhanced compared to wild-type and single knockout animals. Both voltage-dependent inactivation (VDI) and calcium-dependent inactivation (CDI) are significantly increased, with VDI approximately two times larger and CDI approximately six times larger than in WT IHCs. Transgenic expression of CaBP2 leads to partial recovery of this phenotype.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this core finding. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'bring compelling evidence that CaBP 1 and 2 are both involved in the inactivation of the calcium current.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the data is convincing that Cabp1/2 is required for reducing CDI in cochlear hair cells.' Reviewer 3 states the authors 'convincingly demonstrate that both CaBP1 and CaBP2 together confer a lack of inactivation.' The evidence from patch-clamp recordings is described as rigorous and well-supported.

results.result: Sustained exocytosis is severely impaired in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs, particularly for long stimuli and at depolarized holding potentials. The reduction in exocytosis cannot be fully explained by reduced Ca2+ influx alone, suggesting additional impairment in exo- or endocytic processes. AAV-mediated delivery of CaBP2 substantially rescues this exocytosis defect.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently support these findings. Reviewer 1 notes the authors demonstrate 'synaptic release was reduced in the double KO' with 'compelling evidence' from 'cellular up to system level.' Reviewer 2 states 'the data is convincing' regarding the role of CaBPs in 'enabling proper IHC neurotransmitter release.' The rescue experiments are described as believable and well-supported, though Reviewer 2 notes the lack of sham surgery controls as a minor limitation.

results.result: Recovery from inactivation is slowed in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs, particularly after prolonged mild stimulation. After a 500-ms depolarization, recovery is relatively fast in both DKO and WT, but after prolonged sine wave stimulation, recovery is slowest in DKO IHCs. The authors propose this reflects entry into a 'deep-state' of inactivation with very slow recovery.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically flags Figure 4B results as potentially overinterpreted, noting 'without comparison to a sham surgery, it is not known if this result could be a subtle result of the surgery or indeed due to the Cabp2 expression.' The authors acknowledge this limitation in added text. While the data show differences in recovery kinetics, the interpretation regarding the mechanism and the role of CaBP2 overexpression in slowing recovery remains uncertain without proper controls.

results.result: In vivo single-unit recordings from spiral ganglion neurons (SGNs) in Cabp1/2-DKO mice show drastically reduced spontaneous and sound-evoked firing rates, increased latency and jitter, strong adaptation, and strong dependence on stimulation rates. These deficits improve when stimulus repetition rate is lowered.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these in vivo findings as part of the comprehensive evidence. Reviewer 1 notes the authors demonstrate 'depressed activity within the auditory nerve' as a consequence of the cellular defects. The editor's summary describes the work as having 'rigorous in vitro and in vivo physiological experiments.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the data is convincing' regarding the overall phenotype from cellular to systems level.

results.result: Transgenic expression of CaBP2 via AAV-mediated gene delivery leads to substantial recovery of IHC synaptic function and hearing sensitivity in Cabp1/2-DKO mice, including improved ABR thresholds, increased wave amplitudes, and shortened latencies. However, recovery is partial rather than complete, particularly for threshold responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers support the rescue findings while noting limitations. Reviewer 2 states 'in most cases, the improvement of hearing function with AAV injection is believable and should be attributed to the cabp2 function,' though notes the lack of sham surgery controls. Reviewer 3 confirms 're-admission of CaBP2 through viral gene transfer into the inner ear of double-knockout mice largely restored hearing function, normal Ca2+ current properties, and exocytosis.' The partial nature of the rescue is acknowledged by reviewers as appropriately discussed by the authors.

results.result: Cabp1/2-DKO animals exhibit severe hearing impairment as measured by auditory brainstem responses (ABRs), with highly elevated thresholds for tone bursts and clicks, greatly reduced amplitudes, and absence of detectable ABR wave I. The phenotype worsens with age.
results.evaluation: Reviewers consistently affirm the hearing impairment findings. Reviewer 3 describes the animals as 'a deaf mouse model' and notes the authors 'convincingly demonstrate' the phenotype. The editor's summary states the work 'substantially advances our understanding' with 'compelling' evidence. The ABR data are treated as robust measures of the systems-level consequences of the cellular defects.

results.result: Immunohistochemical analysis reveals normal presynaptic CaV1.3 clustering and ribbon synapse abundance in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs, but increased intensities of pre- and postsynaptic markers and reduced BK channel cluster size. These morphological changes can be partially reversed by viral expression of CaBP2.
results.evaluation: The editor's summary explicitly mentions 'state-of-the-art microscopy' as part of the compelling evidence. Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors improved the quality of the figures as requested,' indicating the microscopy data met reviewer standards. The morphological findings are treated as supporting evidence for the functional defects rather than as primary conclusions.

results.result: The functions of CaBP1 and CaBP2 partially overlap at the IHC ribbon synapse. Together they provide sufficient attenuation of channel inactivation to sustain Ca2+ currents and exocytosis required for indefatigable neurotransmission, as evidenced by the much more severe phenotype in double knockouts compared to single knockouts.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this interpretation. Reviewer 1 states 'this study clearly points that CaBP1 is involved in the calcium current inactivation' and notes the overlapping functions. Reviewer 3 describes the finding as 'surprising given the mild phenotype of the single knockouts, which has been published by the authors before.' The comparison across genotypes is treated as a key strength demonstrating functional redundancy.

results.result: Cochlear amplification by outer hair cells is largely preserved in Cabp1/2-DKO animals, as assessed by distortion product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), though about half of DKO animals show reduced DPOAE amplitudes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not raise concerns about the DPOAE data or the interpretation that outer hair cell function is relatively preserved. This finding is treated as supporting evidence that the primary defect is in inner hair cell synaptic function rather than cochlear amplification, consistent with the overall narrative.

results.result: CaBP1/2-deficient IHCs show a significant shift in voltage-dependent activation of Ca2+ channels (altered V0.5 and slope), which persists even after re-expression of CaBP2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about altered activation properties. The data are presented with appropriate statistical analysis (p < 0.0001) and are treated as part of the comprehensive characterization of channel biophysics in the different genotypes.

results.result: The extent of channel inactivation and impairment of IHC synaptic exocytosis in Cabp1/2-DKO animals is strongly dependent on the extent of IHC stimulation, with more pronounced effects at depolarized holding potentials that mimic physiological conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 specifically praises this aspect: 'while changing the holding potential worsen the secretion, it completely changes the kinetics of the inactivation recovery. It alerts the reader that probing different experimental conditions that may be closer to physiology are better suited to uncover any deleterious phenotype.' This is treated as a methodological strength that reveals the full extent of the phenotype.

results.result: The severe exocytosis defect observed in Cabp1/2-DKO IHCs was not observed in single Cabp1 or Cabp2 knockout animals in previous studies, indicating that the two proteins can partially compensate for each other's absence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparison to previous single knockout studies. Reviewer 3 explicitly notes this is 'surprising given the mild phenotype of the single knockouts.' The comparison is treated as important context for understanding the functional redundancy between CaBP1 and CaBP2.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on enhanced channel inactivation in DKO mice (C4, C13, C46-48, C54-57). Both evaluations find the patch-clamp evidence compelling and well-supported. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative measurements and statistical rigor, while peer reviewers highlight the convincing nature of the evidence across all three reviewers.

Strong agreement on impaired exocytosis findings (C6, C37-38, C58-79). Both find capacitance measurements convincing. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with detailed quantitative analysis, while peer reviewers also support but note minor limitation of lacking sham surgery controls. Peer review includes C180 not in OpenEval result.

Disagreement on recovery kinetics interpretation (C5, C82-89). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED despite noting some speculation about 'deep-state' inactivation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, specifically flagging Figure 4B as potentially overinterpreted without sham surgery controls. Both acknowledge the limitation but differ in overall confidence.

Agreement on in vivo SGN recording findings (C8-10, C119-137). Both evaluations support these systems-level measurements. OpenEval covers more specific claims (C118-138) while peer review focuses on subset (C119-137, C141). Both treat the data as rigorous evidence of auditory nerve dysfunction.

Agreement on rescue experiments (C11-12, C41-43, C115-117, C164-166, C222). Both rate as SUPPORTED while acknowledging limitations. OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive cellular and systems-level improvements. Peer reviewers note the believable improvements but mention lack of sham controls as minor limitation. Both acknowledge partial rescue appropriately.

Agreement on hearing impairment via ABR (C36, C104-111). Both evaluations strongly support these findings. OpenEval includes C138 not in peer result. Peer reviewers describe the mouse as a 'deaf model' and treat ABR data as robust. Both view this as clear systems-level evidence.

Agreement on immunohistochemistry findings (C90-93, C96-101). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of synapse morphology and compensatory changes. Peer reviewers mention 'state-of-the-art microscopy' and note improved figure quality, treating morphological data as supporting evidence for functional defects.

Agreement on functional redundancy between CaBP1 and CaBP2 (C44-45, C143, C173). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval includes C172 not in peer result. Both evaluations treat the comparison of single vs double knockout phenotypes as key evidence for partial redundancy. Peer reviewers note this finding is 'surprising' given mild single knockout phenotypes.

Agreement on DPOAE findings indicating preserved OHC function (C112-114). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate acknowledgment of variability. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns, treating this as supporting evidence that the primary defect is in IHC synaptic function rather than cochlear amplification.

Agreement on altered activation properties (C51-53). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the finding is surprising and opposite to heterologous expression expectations, suggesting compensatory changes. Peer reviewers accept the data with appropriate statistical analysis without challenging the interpretation.

Agreement on activity-dependent worsening and holding potential effects (C139-140, C75-76, C80-81, C203-206). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, treating predictions as reasonable extrapolations. Peer reviewers also support, with Reviewer 1 specifically praising this methodological approach as revealing the full phenotype under physiologically relevant conditions. OpenEval result includes additional claims not in peer result.

OpenEval found expression data supporting CaBP1/CaBP2 focus (C1-2, C34-35, C144-145) as SUPPORTED based on citations to prior work. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though this rationale is implicitly accepted by reviewers.

OpenEval rates mechanistic hypotheses about BK channels and exocytosis efficiency (C102-103, C185, C188, C192) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative proposals for future research. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found addressing these mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval rates clinical predictions and gene therapy recommendations (C216-221) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are reasonable extrapolations but speculative regarding human patients. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found addressing these clinical implications.

OpenEval rates mechanistic interpretations of recovery kinetics (C193-199) as UNCERTAIN, noting considerable speculation despite plausible hypotheses. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation found, though related recovery data (C82-89) are addressed in peer R3 with UNCERTAIN rating.

Peer reviewers support comparison to previous single knockout studies (C39-40, C142, C178-179), treating this as important context for understanding functional redundancy. No corresponding specific OpenEval result found, though related redundancy claims (C44-45, C143, C173) are addressed in OpenEval R8.
